## Paper

## Abstract

Accumulating evidence indicates that both putative promoters and enhancers can exert dual promoter and enhancer functions. However, how these activities are related within individual elements and what determines this dual functionality remain poorly understood. We developed a massively parallel dual reporter assay that enables simultaneous assessment of the intrinsic promoter and enhancer potential exerted by the same sequence. Parallel quantification for thousands of elements reveal that canonical human promoters and enhancers can act as both promoters and enhancers under the same contexts, and that promoter activity may be necessary but not sufficient for enhancer function. Perturbations to element transcription factor binding motifs lead to disruptions in both activities, implicating a shared syntax for the two regulatory functions. Combinations of elements with different minimal promoters reveal reciprocal activity modulation, which, together with a strong correlation between promoter and enhancer functions, imply a bidirectional feedback loop to sustain environments of high transcriptional activity. Finally, we validate this reciprocity and correlation in situ using CRISPR activation at the human β-globin locus. Our approach reveals that the functional convergence between promoters and enhancers arises from a shared regulatory logic and sequence syntax, advancing a unified model for regulatory element biology.

---

## Introduction

Cellular processes are precisely controlled through complex gene expression programs that integrate signals from gene-proximal promoters and gene-distal enhancers. Traditionally, promoters and enhancers have been considered separate classes of transcriptional regulatory elements (TREs), often distinguished by their functions, chromatin environments, and genomic locations. Increasing evidence, however, has revealed broad similarities between both the architecture and function of these two regulatory elements, complicating their classification as distinct types1,2.

Promoters are classically defined as DNA sequences that drive RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription initiation at gene-proximal transcription start sites (TSS)3. The region around the TSS (typically defined as the ±50 base pair (bp) region surrounding the TSS) is known as the core promoter, which contains core promoter motifs, such as the Goldberg-Hogness box (TATA box) and the Initiator (Inr)4. These motifs are recognized and bound by general transcription factors (GTFs), such as TBP and TFIIB, that recruit and assemble the RNAPII pre-initiation complex (PIC). RNAPII transcription initiation, promoter-proximal pausing, and pause-release into productive elongation are further facilitated by gene-, cell-, and state-specific transcription factors (TFs) and co-factors that bind at the promoter and at other regulatory sequences such as enhancers to regulate gene transcription5.

Conversely, enhancers are defined as DNA sequences that stimulate transcription at a distance, irrespective of their position and orientation with respect to their target gene6. The first enhancer discovered was a 72 bp sequence from the SV40 genome that could dramatically increase the transcription of the β-globin gene in a distance- and orientation-independent manner7–9. Enhancers were soon after discovered in Mammalia10 and are now recognized as key elements in the regulation of eukaryotic transcription. Today, enhancers are generally thought of as TF-binding regulatory regions that come into proximity to their target gene promoters via three-dimensional DNA looping11.

Numerous findings now point to promoters and enhancers being far more similar than previously thought, spearheaded by the discovery of widespread transcription at enhancer loci12,13. Detailed characterization has revealed that when active, both are encompassed within nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs), bound by sequence-specific TFs that facilitate the assembly of PICs at core promoter regions, and undergo divergent transcription initiation and pausing, with protein-coding gene promoters divergently transcribing mRNAs and upstream antisense RNAs (uaRNAs) in either direction and enhancers divergently transcribing enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) in both14–19. These remarkable similarities in chromatin and sequence architecture have led to a proposed unified model for transcriptional regulatory elements2,14,16.

Prior attempts at defining promoters and enhancers have largely assumed that their functions are distinct and non-overlapping. However, enhancers possess intrinsic promoter potential12,13,20, and numerous studies are now reporting that promoters can exert distal enhancer activity21–24. Understanding how these two activities within the same element relate and elucidating their shared determinants is necessary to ensure that current models of gene regulation capture the full complexity of regulatory element functionality.

To date, experiments that measure both the promoter and enhancer potentials of the same set of sequences are lacking. One of the few studies to have employed such a strategy on a large scale was Nguyen et al., which used separate massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) to measure promoter and enhancer activities for the same elements25. This attempt, however, like all existing MPRAs, inherently decouples the intrinsic promoter and enhancer potential from one another, regulatory potentials that are likely interrelated in their native contexts. One method developed by Mikhaylichenko et al. detected promoter and enhancer activities simultaneously, though it was limited to a small test set of elements given the utilization of fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) as their functional readout26.

For these reasons, we developed a Quantitative Unifying Assay for Simultaneously Active Regulatory Regions by sequencing (QUASARR-seq), a massively parallel dual reporter assay that allows for the simultaneous measurement of intrinsic promoter and enhancer potentials exerted by the same element, for thousands of elements in a single experiment. We perform systematic functional comparisons between intrinsic promoter and enhancer functions exerted by canonical promoter and enhancer elements, revealing a degree of entanglement between the two activities, across element types. Our findings suggest that regulatory potential is embedded within element sequences, with impairments in element promoter activity showing compounding effects by also impairing enhancer function. Finally, using combinations of elements with different minimal promoters (minPs), we find that paired elements exert reciprocal regulatory influences to establish promoter and enhancer function of each element, and validate this phenomenon in situ using CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) data at a human enhancer-promoter pair. Our results support the principle that promoters and enhancers are not separate classes of regulatory elements, with their functional convergence underpinned by shared regulatory logic and sequence syntax.

---

## Results

To investigate the relation and determinants of promoter and enhancer element dual functionality, we sampled a set of TREs in the human immortalized myelogenous leukemia cell line K-562. We previously demonstrated that Precision Run-On and capped nascent RNA sequencing (PRO-cap), a technique that maps TSSs genome-wide by capturing and sequencing the 5′ capped ends of nascent transcripts, provides high predictive performance using 500 bp distance cutoffs from GENCODE annotations, a high-quality, comprehensive reference database of human genes, to distinguish promoter and enhancer elements (see Methods)27,28. Thus, we selected candidate active promoters defined as GENCODE-proximal PRO-cap TSSs and candidate active enhancers as distal TSSs (Fig. 1a). Additionally, we selected a set of candidate inactive promoters defined as proximal PRO-cap untranscribed DNase-seq DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs) and candidate inactive enhancers as distal untranscribed DHSs. In total, we tested 2,151 elements, ranging from 65 to 703 bp, with a median length of 254 bp (Supplementary Fig. 1a).

Hereafter, for clarity, we use the terms ‘promoter activity’ to refer to the candidate TREs ability to drive transcription locally (i.e., initiation at the TRE) and ‘enhancer activity’ to refer to the candidate TREs ability to drive transcription from a distance (i.e., initiation at the minP).

QUASARR-seq simultaneously measures an element’s intrinsic promoter and enhancer activity

To systematically evaluate the functional duality of transcriptional regulatory elements, we developed a Quantitative Unifying Assay for Simultaneously Active Regulatory Regions by sequencing (QUASARR-seq), a massively parallel dual reporter assay that enables the simultaneous measurement of intrinsic promoter and enhancer potentials exerted by the same regulatory element molecule (Fig. 1a). QUASARR-seq adopts the principles of classical reporter assays where candidate regulatory sequences are cloned into expression vectors but incorporates two functional reporter systems each used to independently quantify promoter and enhancer activity for the same sequence (see Methods). Enhancer activity measurements are obtained by the reporter system positioned upstream of the TRE that contains a minP that drives the expression of enhancer activity barcodes (eaBCs) located within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of an enhancer activity transcript (eaT). Similarly, promoter activity measurements are obtained by the reporter system positioned downstream of the TRE where the TRE itself drives the expression of promoter activity barcodes (paBCs) located within the 5′ UTR of a promoter activity transcript (paT). As in all MPRAs, QUASARR-seq quantifies activity as the ratio of counts of aBC RNA transcripts to aBC DNA input vectors, from which boost indices are calculated by basal expression level normalization using negative controls (see Methods).

QUASARR-seq promoter activity measurements [log2 (RNA paBCs/DNA paBCs)] across replicates demonstrated a high degree of reproducibility (R2 = 0.98; Fig. 1b). As expected, promoter activity varied significantly across GENCODE classes, with PRO-cap transcribed proximal elements (i.e., active promoters) exhibiting the highest activity, followed by transcribed distal elements (i.e., active enhancers), and with untranscribed elements and negative control open reading frames (ORFs) exhibiting little or no activity, respectively (P-value < 0.001, Student’s t-test; Fig. 1c). Interestingly, many of the proximal elements with the highest promoter activities were found to correspond to the promoters of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). The top three included: 1. the divergent promoter for LINC01138 (lncRNA)/RNVU1-21 (snRNA) and ENSG00000224481 (uncharacterized lncRNA), 2. the promoter for RNVU1-2A (snRNA), and 3. the divergent promoter for SNHG1 (lncRNA) and SLC3A2 (protein coding).

---

## Methods

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

As a followed up of previous studies [Nguyen, T.A. et al. High-throughput functional comparison of promoter and enhancer activities. Genome Res 26, 1023-33 (2016) and Mikhaylichenko, O. et al. The degree of enhancer or promoter activity is reflected by the levels and directionality of eRNA transcription. Genes Dev 32, 42-57 (2018)], the originality of this manuscript is that both enhancers and promoters’ activity has been quantified (high-throughput sequencing using barcodes) together using the same reporter system (QUASARR-Seq). The limitation of the study is that it is not done in a chromatin context (plasmid), and this is acknowledged (briefly) in the Discussion section.
Major comments
After reading the abstract, it is still difficult to understand what the main conclusions are. A shorten version of the abstract may help to focus on the key take home message. Same as for the last paragraph of the introduction (lanes 85-90).
While I don’t have the capacity and the skills to check all the bioinformatics and statistics in this study, the work presented here is colossal and good fit for the journal. However, the narrative is very explorative by testing a variety of hypothesis which disconnects the reading interest. This reflects the above comments about the abstract. The last part of the manuscript (Discussion Section) ends the same way by the lack of key highlights.
The distinction between enhancers and promoters is always blurred and this is well presented in the introduction. Enhancers are (usually) bidirectional and promoters mostly unidirectional (as these must tell the PolII machinery which direction the coding gene is). In a chromatin context, they can be distinguished by deposition of high H3K4me1 at enhancers and high H3K4me3 at promoters. However, in contrast to enhancers and regardless of chromatin context, promoters have been classified in subgroups based on consensus sequences located at specific distances from TSS (e.g. TATA box at -25bp, CAAT Box at -75bp etc…). Some promoters have CpG Islands (usually constitutive, unless repressed by CpG), some have a TATA Box, and others an Initiator element (INR). Without additional lab work, the authors may find benefit by pushing the analysis further in separating the effect of all promoters tested based on these categories and hopefully find sometime more conclusive.
Additional comment (for future studies)
Enhancers are usually primed first, suggesting that the ‘transcription signal’ is primarily launched remotely to eventually reach the promoter. In the future, perhaps a key experiment on a single locus would be to swap enhancer and promoter and see what happens, but this is out of the scope of this manuscript.

### Reviewer 2

The study by Paramo et al. investigated enhancer and promoter activity of human transcriptional regulatory elements (TREs) with QUASARR-seq, a newly developed massively parallel reporter assay. The TREs were defined by nascent transcription start sites, which were demonstrated to be good predictors of regulatory activity. The authors found that TREs often drive both distal and proximal expression, i.e., the promoter and enhancer activities of the same element are often correlated. The regulatory activity can be modulated by different minimal promoters.
I found that the data are sufficient to support the authors’ conclusion. The study strengthened the previous notion that promoters and enhancers might not be functionally distinct elements. Once in a microenvironment with high regulatory activity (or the “all-by-all” model as the authors put it), i.e., high concentration of RNAP, TFs, open chromatin, etc., the regulatory elements may function either as promoters or enhancers.
However, it was not very surprising that most TREs showed correlated promoter and enhancer activities, especially when the enhancer activity was evaluated by its ability to drive expression of a nearby minP in a synthetic construct. Traditionally, one feature that distinguishes enhancers from promoters is that its ability to drive expression at a distance. From the paper, it was not very clear how far apart the TREs were from the minPs and whether the physical distance should be considered when we evaluate the distal regulatory activity, which could be added to the methods and discussion respectively. Another discerning feature of enhancers is its cell-type specificity, which is not evaluated by the current assay but might worth discussion. Furthermore, it was not surprising that the regulatory activity can be modulated by minPs, either. It would be interesting to learn what sequence features, besides GC content, were involved in the interaction, if there were enough data for such analysis.
In terms of clarity, I would appreciate more details in terms of the library design, e.g., how long the TREs are, how many TREs were included in the library, how they are chosen (Random? Representatives of different cell types? Different information content?), if they consist of known TF binding sites, etc.
Minor points:
Line 96: GENCODE annotations: it would be helpful to explain what they are for people who are not familiar with this database. Similarly, the PRO-cap technique needs to be explained on first mention (what is the abbreviation short for?).
Fig. 1a: it would be helpful to show “candidate active promoters” “candidate active enhancers” “candidate inactive promoters” and “candidate inactive enhancers” as a table, along with their corresponding diagrams. Also, it wasn’t very clear what the peak height means in the diagrams and how it is related to proximal/distal classification.
Fig. 1c: is “GENCODE distal & PRO-cap untranscribed” equivalent to “Distal DHS & PRO-cap untranscribed” as in Fig. 1a and Line 100? In general, I was a bit confused about how GENCODE class was defined and how it was related to DHS.
Line 219: SOLARR-seq was only introduced after line 290, so referencing the SOLARR-seq data here is a bit confusing.
Line 350: “a small delta boost index…”: it might be clearer to say “a low delta boost index” or “a negative delta boost index indicated a disrupting effect”.
Line 354: it would be nice to report effect size along with the P-value.
Fig. 5: “a, b, c” could be moved to the top-left corner of each panel. Legend for (a) was not very clear in terms of what “left” and “right” refer to. Also, there is no error bar or scatter points in (a) that indicate the distribution of data.
Line 685: “R” was not defined. Should it be “Bal”?
Extended Data Figs and Supplementary figures: usually, extended data figures go into supplementary. So, it was a bit confusing that some supp. figures are named “extended data fig” and others “supplementary fig”.

### Reviewer 3

Evidence has been accumulating that enhancers and promoters may in fact be two sides of the same coin. This manuscript systematically addresses this hypothesis by testing E and P activity of a collection of regulatory elements simultaneously in a dual reporter construct. This is novel and exciting. The design of the experiments is very elegant, and the (often challenging) computational analyses were done with great care. The findings support the hypothesis that E and P activities of single regulatory elements are indeed tightly linked, and the authors favor the interpretation that E activity requires P activity - which seems reasonable given the results with a set of mutants. Moreover, they provide evidence that three Ps differ in their dynamic range of response to Es, and reciprocally affect E activity to different degrees. Overall, this manuscript is of high quality and of substantial novelty, and will be of interest to a broad readership interested in the fundamental biology of Es and Ps. That said, I have a few points that could strengthen it further.
Major points:
line 205+: Potential readthrough of the pA sites is indeed a risk. I did not understand the logic of the orientation analysis. How can this estimate readthrough? Please explain better; perhaps a cartoon could help? If I understand it correctly, the results point to some degree of (rho = 0.16) of readthrough? Then the authors' conclusion seems a bit too strong: "supporting the case that the high correlation of promoter and enhancer activities is not an artifact of measuring the same function"". Please tone down. This conclusion could perhaps be strengthened by RT-qPCR of plasmid backbone sequences downstream of the 2nd pA, or of sequences in EGFP when no TRE is inserted? Or, perhaps simpler, what is the ratio paBC over eaBC counts in RNA when no TRE is inserted?
One of the most interesting concepts arising from this work is that promoters may reciprocally activate nearby enhancers (Figure 5d). But of course the experimental setting used here is quite artificial (as acknowledged in the Discussion). It seems to me that it should not be too difficult to test the P-->E effect in a native genomic context: delete a P by CRISPR/ and test whether the activity of a nearby E (using ATAC-seq, H3K27ac or PRO-Cap as proxy readout) is reduced. Possibly such data is already publicly available, but no-one bothered to look at it this way? Addition of a small set of such experiments could greatly strengthen this manuscript. I should point out that even a negative result would be insightful (albeit a bit disappointing, of course); publication should not depend on a positive result.
The P and E boost indices show a substantial difference in dynamic range (Extended data figure 1a). The authors then z-normalize these to enable the calculation of a P/E balance index. Although these differences in dynamic range are puzzling, this seems a reasonable approach when only a single minP is analyzed in the first part of the manuscript. However, I found this much more difficult to interpret when the three minPs have different dynamic ranges - which I gather from figure 6a (but it would be good to show the equivalent of extended data fig 1a for the three minPs). With these differences in dynamic range, can the balance indices still be compared? Is it fair to remove these differences by z-normalization? The interpretation becomes even more complicated to me when the authors switch to ranked balance indices and show quite puzzling scatter plots (figs 6c,d,e). My overall feeling is that the authors push the data analysis a little too far in figure 6; I am afraid that most readers may not be able to deeply understand these results. Because the manuscript is already quite long and detailed, I suggest to remove Figure 6; this will help to focus the manuscript on the key messages.
Minor points:

### Reviewer 4

Multiple studies in recent years have demonstrated that enhancers and promoters are much more similar than previously regarded. Nevertheless, experimental settings that enable the quantitative measurements of both the promoter and enhancer potentials of the same set of sequences are lacking. The authors have elegantly designed and developed “Quantitative Unifying Assay for Simultaneously Active Regulatory Regions by sequencing (QUASARR-seq)”, a massively parallel dual reporter assay that enables the simultaneous measurement of the intrinsic promoter and enhancer potentials exerted by the same element.
The authors rigorously demonstrate that canonical human promoters and enhancers can indeed act as both promoters and enhancers under the same contexts, and that promoter activity may be necessary but insufficient for enhancer function. They examined whether the regulatory potential is embedded within element sequences and discovered that variants with strong clinical/functional evidence for imparing promoter activity, also impair enhancer activity. Using combinations of transcription regulatory elements with three different minimal promoters (GAPDH, MYC and APOBEC3F) they identified reciprocal regulatory effects between the associated elements, and a strong positive correlation between promoter and enhancer activities. They further discovered that the promoter-enhancer activity balance is determined by both sequence-intrinsic properties and contextual regulatory effects.
The study addresses a fundamental question in gene regulation and will be of broad interest to researchers in the field. It is novel, elegantly designed and rigorously executed, making it highly suitable for Nature Communications.
Minor Comments:
1. I suggest elaborating in the discussion on the following issues:
a. The study was conducted using the human K562 cell line. How might the findings differ if the study were performed in a different cellular context?
b. Potential outcomes if the cells were induced to differentiate
2. Cells were harvested 6 hours post electroporation. While this time point is appropriate for capturing immediate early responses, it may not be optimal for assaying enhancer function. I suggest including a brief rationale for the choice of the 6-hour time point.
3. Fig. 1 legend - indicate which minimal promoter was used
4. Fig. 5a legend – left and right should be top and bottom

Author We thank the reviewer for highlighting the originality of our approach.
Response
To clarify, QUASARR-seq goes a step beyond quantifying promoters’ and
enhancers’ singular activities using the same reporter system. Instead, it enables
simultaneous measurement of both promoter and enhancer functions exerted by the
same sequence. For each tested element (including annotated promoters and
enhancers) we assess its capacity to drive transcription locally (promoter activity)
and its capacity to stimulate transcription of another element from a distance
(enhancer activity), in parallel. This design enables a direct and unbiased element-
wide comparison of regulatory potential.
We also acknowledge, as noted in the Discussion, that the assay is plasmid-based
and therefore does not fully capture chromatin-mediated regulation. Nevertheless,
we believe this system provides valuable information on the intrinsic functional
capabilities of gene regulatory sequences.

Author We thank the reviewer for the opportunity to clarify our main objectives and
Response conclusions of our study. The manuscript is organized around three central
questions, inspired by the increasing body of evidence suggesting that both
promoters and enhancers are capable of exerting promoter and enhancer
functionalities.
1. How can the promoter and enhancer activities exerted by the same element
be measured simultaneously?
a. We developed QUASARR-seq, a massively parallel dual reporter
assay that simultaneously measures both activities exerted from the
same sequence.
2. What is the relationship between promoter and enhancer activities within
individual elements?
a. Annotated promoters and enhancers can concurrently exert both
activities under the same contexts and are thus not mutually
exclusive functions of the same element.
b. The two activities exerted by the same element are positively
correlated (i.e., the stronger the element’s enhancer activity, the
stronger its promoter activity).
3. What are the determinants of this dual promoter-enhancer functionality?
a. Promoter activity is necessary for an element to have enhancer
function, but it is not sufficient.
b. Transcript features, including termination signals, defining
annotated promoters and enhancers do not confer regulatory activity.
c. Intrinsic-sequence features, including GC content and transcription
factor motifs, influence both functions in an element, suggesting a
shared sequence syntax.
d. Both activities in an element are modulated by the reciprocal
regulatory influence of its paired element (i.e., as an enhancer
stimulates its target promoter’s transcription, the promoter in turn
stimulates its enhancer’s transcription).
In all, our results support the unifying conclusion that promoters and enhancers may
not be separate classes of regulatory elements, since a shared regulatory logic and
sequence syntax underlie their functional convergence.
To improve clarity, we have revised the Abstract and the final paragraph of the
Introduction to better emphasize the main conclusions. We hope this reframing
helps convey the main takeaways of the work, and we thank the reviewer again for
the valuable suggestion.
Revised Abstract
Excerpt Accumulating evidence indicates that both promoters and enhancers are capable of
exerting promoter and enhancer functions; however, the relationship between these
two activities within individual elements and the determinants of this dual
functionality remain poorly understood. We developed a massively parallel dual
reporter assay that enables simultaneous assessment of the intrinsic promoter and
enhancer potential exerted by the same sequence. Parallel quantification for
thousands of elements reveals that canonical human promoters and enhancers can
act as both promoters and enhancers under the same contexts, and that promoter
activity may be necessary but not sufficient for enhancer function. Perturbations to
2
element transcription factor binding motifs lead to disruptions in both activities,
implicating a shared syntax for the two regulatory functions. Combinations of
elements with different minimal promoters reveal reciprocal activity modulation,
which, together with a strong correlation between promoter and enhancer functions,
imply a bidirectional feedback loop to sustain environments of high transcriptional
activity. Finally, we validate this reciprocity and correlation in situ using CRISPR
activation at the human β-globin locus. Our approach reveals that the functional
convergence between promoters and enhancers arises from a shared regulatory logic
and sequence syntax, advancing a unified model for regulatory element biology.
Introduction
For these reasons, we developed a Quantitative Unifying Assay for Simultaneously
Active Regulatory Regions by sequencing (QUASARR-seq), a massively parallel
dual reporter assay that allows for the simultaneous measurement of intrinsic
promoter and enhancer potentials exerted by the same element, for thousands of
elements in a single experiment. We perform systematic functional comparisons
between intrinsic promoter and enhancer functions exerted by canonical promoter
and enhancer elements, revealing a degree of entanglement between the two
activities, across element types. Our findings suggest that regulatory potential is
embedded within element sequences, with impairments in element promoter activity
showing compounding effects by also impairing enhancer function. Finally, using
combinations of elements with different minimal promoters (minPs), we find that
paired elements exert reciprocal regulatory influences to establish promoter and
enhancer functions of each element, and validate this phenomenon in situ using
CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) data at a human enhancer-promoter pair. Our results
support the principle that promoters and enhancers are not separate classes of
regulatory elements, with their functional convergence underpinned by shared
regulatory logic and sequence syntax.

Revised Discussion
Excerpt Our findings further challenge the conventional distinction between promoters and
enhancers and instead support a unified model arising from a shared regulatory logic
and sequence syntax present across element classes. Using QUASARR-seq, we
demonstrate that both canonical promoters and enhancers can drive transcription
locally and at a distance under the same regulatory contexts, finding evidence that
promoter activity may be necessary, but not sufficient for enhancer function. This
dual potential is unifyingly rooted by intrinsic sequence features and regulatory
context.
The strong positive correlation between promoter and enhancer activities exerted by
the same element could be indicative of a positive feedback loop, where reciprocal
modulation between associated elements reinforces their regulatory functions. This
bidirectional feedback may increase and maintain local concentrations of RNAPII,
TFs, and co-activators to establish environments with high transcriptional activity.
To this end, we propose an ‘all-by-all’ model for transcriptional regulatory elements
(Fig. 6g), in which all elements (both canonical gene promoters and enhancers)
exhibit functional duality to reciprocally regulate one another. This framework
extends existing hub/condensate models by adding a bidirectional feedback
component, where rather than unidirectional enhancer-to-promoter activation, all
elements (i.e., enhancer-to-promoter, promoter-to-enhancer, enhancer-to-enhancer,
and promoter-to-promoter) reinforce one another through shared recruitment of
factors, sustaining self-organized environments of high transcriptional activity. We
note that the concept of regulatory element co-regulation is supported by a recent
study1. Using single-cell live imaging in flies, Levo et al. elegantly demonstrated
that physically distant promoters can undergo coordinated transcriptional bursting.
These findings indicate that regulatory crosstalk between TREs may be a
widespread feature of gene regulation in vivo.
Variants that disrupted promoter activity simultaneously impaired enhancer
function, revealing the interconnected nature of these activities. This shared
susceptibility has significant implications for understanding disease-associated
variants as they may have compounding effects on gene regulation. These findings
may underscore the need for therapeutic approaches that address the dual roles of
regulatory elements.
While our study provides compelling evidence for a unified framework of TREs,
we acknowledge several limitations. Read-through past the first pA accounted for
~16% of egfp signal. Next generation designs could integrate capped RNA
enrichment to detect transcripts arising exclusively from the TREs and enable
positional TSS mapping, similar to the recently developed TSS-MPRA2,3.
Moreover, the transient nature of our assay does not fully recapitulate endogenous
4
chromatin dynamics that influence regulatory interactions, in particular the much
longer genomic distances spanned by enhancer-promoter contacts. Additionally,
broader testing of TREs, minPs, and mutants of the two will be essential to validate
and extend our findings and further elucidate the contextual factors that shape
functional duality. Future work should move toward in vivo models and explore
diverse cellular contexts, including shifts with cell identity and induced
differentiation. Still, we argue that a reductionist system that can isolate and dissect
activities like QUASARR-seq is essential for elucidating fundamental principles of
regulatory element logic as complex endogenous systems can be subjected to
immense regulatory confounders.
To this end, our study advances our understanding of transcriptional regulation by
demonstrating that promoters and enhancers are not separate classes of regulatory
elements, as their functional convergence is underpinned by a shared regulatory
logic and sequence syntax. This paradigm shift provides new insights into the
mechanisms of gene regulation and the functional consequences of regulatory
variants in health and disease.

Reviewer The distinction between enhancers and promoters is always blurred and this is well
Comment presented in the introduction. Enhancers are (usually) bidirectional and promoters
mostly unidirectional (as these must tell the PolII machinery which direction the
coding gene is). In a chromatin context, they can be distinguished by deposition of
high H3K4me1 at enhancers and high H3K4me3 at promoters. However, in contrast

subgroups based on consensus sequences located at specific distances from TSS
(e.g. TATA box at -25bp, CAAT Box at -75bp etc…). Some promoters have CpG
Islands (usually constitutive, unless repressed by CpG), some have a TATA Box,
and others an Initiator element (INR). Without additional lab work, the authors may
find benefit by pushing the analysis further in separating the effect of all promoters
tested based on these categories and hopefully find sometime more conclusive.
Author We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed comment and the opportunity to clarify key
Response points regarding the distinction between enhancers and promoters.
histone modifications like H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 provide a strict, categorical
distinction between enhancers and promoters. Instead, several lines of evidence
suggest that these marks scale with local transcriptional activity, irrespective of
regulatory class:
1. In human cells, we have shown that histone marks at enhancers and
promoters scale with Pol II intensity (Core & Martins et al.1).
2. In both Drosophila and mESCs, most active enhancers harbor H3K4me3
rather than H3K4me1 and the level of H3K4 methylation corresponds to the
amount of transcription at that locus (Henriques et al.2).
3. Similarly, H3K4me1:H3K4me3 ratios and H3K4me1 levels are negatively
associated with endogenous CAGE expression levels in flies (Rennie &
Dalby et al.3).
These data suggest that chromatin-based annotations may more accurately reflect
the level of promoter activity at that locus rather than fundamentally distinguishing
between enhancers and promoters. Since enhancers generally exhibit lower levels
of intrinsic promoter activity and thus show distinct histone mark profiles, studies
such as Henriques et al. demonstrate that when enhancers are highly active, these
chromatin marks converge with those typically seen at promoters, limiting their
reliability as distinguishing features. This is consistent with our results in this study,
which show that active enhancers also generally exert higher levels of intrinsic
promoter activity, further blurring the distinction between these regulatory
functions.
Second, we appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to further investigate the influence
of core promoter architecture on dual regulatory activity. In response, we calculated
motif match scores (see Methods) for all tested elements (both annotated promoters
and enhancers) within specified windows relative to their GRO-cap-detected TSSs
in K-562 cells, including TATA (-40 to -20 bp), Inr (-2 bp), MTE (+5 to +35 bp),
and DPE (+5 to +35 bp). To assess whether specific core promoter motifs contribute
to establishing either element class (proximal vs. distal) or activity bias (promoter-
dominant, balanced, or enhancer-dominant), we compared motif match scores with
promoter-enhancer balance index categories across GENCODE classes.
As expected, the distributions for proximal (i.e., promoters) and distal (i.e.,
enhancers) TREs showed similar relationships between core promoter motif match
scores and activity balance categories (Supplementary Fig. 4f) consistent with

Still, some differences emerged, primarily across balance index categories. In
proximal TREs, promoter-dominant elements had significantly higher Inr and MTE
scores than balanced elements (P-value < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test with
Bonferroni correction). In distal TREs, promoter-dominant elements also had higher
Inr scores than balanced (P-value < 0.01) in addition to enhancer-dominant (P-value
< 0.001) elements. By contrast, promoter-dominant elements had lower TATA
6
scores than balanced (P-value < 0.001) and enhancer-dominant (P-value < 0.01)
elements, whereas DPE was enriched in balanced relative to enhancer-dominant

Revised Results
Excerpt We next sought to assess whether the positive relationship between promoter and
enhancer functions observed in QUASARR-seq could be validated in an
endogenous genomic context. To this end, we re-analyzed a published CRISPRa
dataset in which the enhancer HS2 was targeted with different dCas9-based
transcriptional activators in HEK293T, including dCas9-VPR, dCas9-SAM, dCas9-
SunTag, dCas9-p300, dCas9-CBP, and dCas9 as a negative control1. In this in situ
context, the enhancer HS2 is located ~30 kb downstream of, and convergent with,
its target gene promoter HBG1. Given that activators exhibit distinct activation
strengths, we examined whether varying levels of enhancer transcription activation
were accompanied by corresponding changes in target promoter transcription.
Targeting of HS2 with the different activators showed a strong positive correlation
between HS2 eRNA activation (i.e., HS2 promoter activity) and HBG1 mRNA
activation (i.e., HS2 enhancer activity, Spearman's ρ = 0.79, P-value < 0.001; Fig.
2b). Together with our findings, these data indicate that the positive correlation
between promoter and enhancer activities holds across endogenous genomic
contexts and distances.
Discussion
While our study provides compelling evidence for a unified framework of TREs,
we acknowledge several limitations. Read-through past the first pA accounted for
~16% of egfp signal. Next generation designs could integrate capped RNA
enrichment to detect transcripts arising exclusively from the TREs and enable
positional TSS mapping, similar to the recently developed TSS-MPRA2,3.
Moreover, the transient nature of our assay does not fully recapitulate endogenous
chromatin dynamics that influence regulatory interactions, in particular the much
longer genomic distances spanned by enhancer-promoter contacts. Additionally,
broader testing of TREs, minPs, and mutants of the two will be essential to validate
and extend our findings and further elucidate the contextual factors that shape
functional duality. Future work should move toward in vivo models and explore
diverse cellular contexts, including shifts with cell identity and induced
differentiation. Still, we argue that a reductionist system that can isolate and dissect
activities like QUASARR-seq is essential for elucidating fundamental principles of
regulatory element logic as complex endogenous systems can be subjected to
immense regulatory confounders.

In this design, TREs are positioned 2,180 bp downstream of the minPs (or 2,916 bp
upstream when traversing the circular backbone), ensuring a fixed distance across

To classify promoter and enhancer elements, we based our approach solely on
transcriptional activity (PRO-cap), chromatin accessibility (DNase-seq), and

enhancers as distal PRO-cap untranscribed DNase-seq DHSs (distance cutoff > 500
bp from GENCODE annotation). Transcribed elements were cloned using

Methods

Cell culture and nucleofection were carried out as described above, except 1 x 106
